extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom leaders, media-watchers and journalism ethics practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A chronicle and analysis of plagiarism and fabrication incidents in journalism (2012), highlighting what went wrong and how newsrooms responded; useful for assessing newsroom ethics, corrections, and prevention practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabricating sources and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not fabricate sources, people, or quotes; fabricated sources/quotes are cited as egregious ethical breaches (examples: Paresh Jha fabricated sources in at least 25 stories; Karen Jeffrey fabricated people and quotes in many stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication should trigger investigations, public disclosure and disciplinary action (suspension/firing). Newsrooms must verify sources and be able to account for named people in stories; inability to find cited people (e.g., "editors have been unable to find 69 people in 34 stories") is a sign of fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism (including serial/recurring theft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present others’ words or ideas as your own; serial plagiarism (repeated theft over time) is a severe offense (examples: serial plagiarists stealing humor columns; theft from The Atlantic Wire, AP, ClickZ, Wikipedia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting plagiarism often relies on outside reporting; when discovered, outlets should acknowledge the misconduct, investigate scope, and take appropriate action (apology, suspension, firing, corrections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper and precise attribution of intellectual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and journalists must adhere to strict standards for properly and precisely attributing intellectual content (quoted from CSIS: "reinforced to everyone at CSIS the importance of adhering to strict standards when it comes to properly and precisely attributing intellectual content").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution entails naming sources, crediting originators, and making clear when material is drawn from another outlet or author; institutions should educate staff and enforce attribution policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks and give reasonable credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Sourcing, the use of quotation marks, and reasonable credit for the work of others are baseline standards (Globe and Mail editor: column "did not meet the standards ... in terms of sourcing, use of quotation marks and reasonable credit for the work of others").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must correctly demarcate quoted material and cite sources; editors should check for proper quotations and credits before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify eyewitness accounts and presence reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports based on claimed eyewitness presence must be verified (example: a reporter wrote about a local council meeting "as if he'd been there when he hadn't"; an intern’s account of witnessing an execution included plagiarized material and was questioned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters should confirm attendance and corroborate eyewitness testimony; failure to verify can lead to fabricated or misleading reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure bylines and author attribution are accurate (no fake bylines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bylines and author credits must reflect who actually produced the work; using fake bylines or misattributing authorship is a serious ethical breach (example: Journatic produced hundreds of stories with fake bylines and in some cases fabricated information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should authenticate contributor identities and ensure transparent byline practices, especially with outsourcing or freelance suppliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in corrections, editor’s notes and apologies
rubrics_metrics.description: When plagiarism/fabrication occurs, outlets should add editor’s notes, apologize, and clearly inform readers of the problem (examples: FoxNews.com added an editor’s note and apology; papers published brief notices or apologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be explicit about the nature of the error, describe remedial steps, and be readily visible; vague or absent corrections undermine accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate accountability and disciplinary action by newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should hold reporters accountable through disciplinary measures (suspension, leave, firing) and not avoid responsibility; the piece criticizes a "lack of accountability by newsrooms" in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary responses should be commensurate with the severity and scope of misconduct and should be accompanied by transparent explanation to the public where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and audit past work after allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations should prompt review of a journalist’s other work (examples: Time/CNN reviewed Fareed Zakaria’s work after plagiarism admission; publishers reviewed Jonah Lehrer’s other works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct systematic audits of the subject’s recent and past output to determine scope of problems; remove or correct additional problematic items and consider severing ties if widespread misconduct is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement prevention measures, policies and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should develop prevention strategies and handling procedures for plagiarism/fabrication (example: group organized by ACES working on an ebook to help newsrooms prevent and handle incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt written policies, provide training, and create checklists/workflows to detect plagiarism and fabrication before publication; use resources (ebooks, training) to institutionalize prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-plagiarism and reuse without disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recycling passages across outlets or reusing one's own previously published text without disclosure is unacceptable (example: Jonah Lehrer repeatedly recycled passages in blog posts and books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose reused material or avoid reuse; editors should flag potential self-plagiarism during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of editorial approach and proper sourcing even for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials and opinion pieces must not appropriate another outlet’s approach or structure without acknowledgment (example: Contra Costa Times editorial was "nearly identical" in approach to a Los Angeles Times piece).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure editorials are original in argument and framing; if influenced by other work, credit or acknowledge inspiration to avoid misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog reporting and external scrutiny improve detection and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent bloggers, media-watch organizations and fact-checkers help surface plagiarism/fabrication (examples: Jim Romenesko, iMediaEthics, Deadspin exposed many cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should welcome or monitor external scrutiny, engage with watchdog findings, and act on credible reports; fostering an environment where issues can be raised improves overall standards.
